paper.title: Persistent Trends or Pandemic Effects? A Multi-Cohort Longitudinal Study on Student Well-being, Inequality, and Educational Transitions
paper.code_data_availability: Data Availability: 'To adhere to data protection agreements, the data, materials, and analytic code necessary to reproduce the analyses presented in this paper are not publicly accessible.' (p. …

registers.role: outcomes (school connectedness, academic self-efficacy), treatment definition (cohort and grade), sample frame

registers.years: reference year 2015 for sociodemographic background; transitions observed within two years of 9th grade
variables_mentioned: immigration background (native Danish, first- or second-generation immigrant background)
socio-economic status (SES), operationalized as highest level of parental education (measured in years of education)
final exam grades in Danish and mathematics (GPA)
transition to upper secondary education (academic track, vocational track, leaving the education system)

linkages: Survey responses combined with register data to include demographic background factors, based on the reference year 2015 for all cohorts
Survey responses from all cohorts merged to create a continuous developmental trajectory spanning grades 5 through 9 for both outcomes, using grade-as-time
Students nested in schools (the hierarchical structure the cluster-adjusted standard errors account for)

sample.universe: Students enrolled in grades 5 through 9 across Danish public schools, surveyed annually by the Danish Student Well-being Questionnaire 2016-2023; the dataset represents approximately 85% of the eligible student population each year
sample.unit_of_observation: student x grade (annual survey wave), with students nested in schools
selection_rules: Three cohorts followed from grade 5 to grade 9: pre-pandemic (2015-2019), early-pandemic (2017-2021) and full-pandemic (2019-2023)
Respondents missing all well-being survey waves were excluded
Missing values on the dependent variable handled by maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) rather than imputation
For the educational-choice analyses, transitions were observed within a two-year period after finishing 9th grade, so the full-pandemic cohort is excluded (transition data not yet available)
Only exam grades are used for all cohorts in the GPA measure, to keep it comparable across cohorts
sample.n_observations: 608,961 person-wave observations in the school-connectedness models and 608,373 in the academic-self-efficacy models (Table 2)

construction_notes: School connectedness: mean score across 7 DSWQ items, 5-point scale from 0 to 4; Cronbach's alpha 0.86-0.87 across years
Academic self-efficacy: mean score across 8 DSWQ items, 5-point scale from 0 to 4; Cronbach's alpha 0.83-0.86 across years
A 'do not want to answer' category is provided in addition to the substantive response categories

GPA = Danish oral exam grade + Danish written, spelling * 0.25 + Danish written, reading * 0.25 + Danish written * 0.5 + Mathematics written, with aids *0.5 + Mathematics written, without aids*0.5 (footnote 2, p. 144)
For the early-pandemic cohort exams were partly disrupted and the Ministry of Education allowed year grades to replace lower exam grades; the paper nonetheless uses exam grades only for all cohorts
Grade-as-time: grade level 5 is the reference category and the pre-pandemic cohort is the reference cohort
All regression models estimated with cluster-adjusted standard errors for students nested in schools; all calculations in Stata 18.1
In 2020 data collection occurred primarily between January 20th and March 20th, prior to the first school lockdown (footnote 1, p. 143)
The proportion of missing responses varied between 8.22 and 59.93% by wave and cohort; the number of respondents ranged from 19,733 (grade 9, pre-pandemic) to 51,716 (grade 5, during-pandemic)

Table 1 reports cohort-specific outcome means on a centred scale (e.g. school connectedness 0.054, academic self-efficacy 0.088 for the pre-pandemic cohort at grade 5) while the 'Total' column is on the raw 0-4 scale (4.090 and 3.627); the outcome modelled in Table 2 and plotted in Fig. 2 appears to be the centred/standardised version, but the paper never says so

claims.statement: Averaged over grades 5–9, the early-pandemic cohort's mean school connectedness differs from the pre-pandemic cohort's by -0.001.

definition.value: Dummy for membership of the early-pandemic cohort (grades 5–9 in 2017–2021), with the pre-pandemic cohort (2015–2019) as the reference category. In Models 1a and 2a, which contain no grade × cohort interactions, this coefficient is the mean cohort difference across grades 5–9.

timing.value: Fixed cohort membership, defined by the calendar years 2017–2021 in which the cohort passed through grades 5–9

definition.value: Composite mean score across the 7 school-connectedness items of the Danish Student Well-being Questionnaire, each answered on a 5-point scale from 0 to 4; the scale measures the degree to which students feel accepted and supported within their school environment (sample items: “Do you like your school?”, “I feel that I belong at this school.”). Higher scores indicate a greater sense of connection to the school; Cronbach’s alpha 0.86–0.87 across years.

timing.value: Measured at each annual spring survey wave, grades 5 through 9 (grade-as-time)

estimand.target_population: Students in the early-pandemic cohort
estimand.time_horizon: mean cohort difference across the five annual measurement points, grades 5 to 9

population.description: Students in grades 5–9 in Danish public schools responding to the annual Danish Student Well-being Questionnaire (DSWQ), in three cohorts followed from grade 5 to grade 9: pre-pandemic (49,252 respondents), early-pandemic (51,716) and full-pandemic (49,765)
population.ages: approximately 11–15 years (mean age at grade 5: 11.7 pre-pandemic, 11.6 early-pandemic, 11.6 full-pandemic)
population.selection: Annual census-type survey administered during school hours to students in grades 5–9 across Danish public schools, representing approximately 85% of the eligible student population each year; respondents missing all well-being survey waves were excluded, and missing values on the dependent variable were handled by maximum likelihood estimation. The proportion of missing responses varied between 8.22 and 59.93% by wave and cohort.

identification.source_of_variation: Comparison of the early-pandemic cohort with the pre-pandemic cohort observed at the same grade levels in earlier calendar years

key_assumptions.assumption: Baseline (grade 5) similarity / comparability of the three cohorts, on which the interpretation of the cohort contrasts relies
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 compares demographics, GPA and baseline outcome values across cohorts with t-tests and chi-squared tests; the authors report the differences as 'generally minor, though in many cases statistically significant'

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends across cohorts prior to the pandemic (the pre-pandemic cohort's grade-by-grade trajectory is the counterfactual trajectory the pandemic cohorts would have followed)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Footnote 3 and Figure 2: 'Figure 2 shows a general pattern of parallel trends across the three cohorts, except for the period between 5th and 6th grade'

key_assumptions.assumption: Missing well-being responses are ignorable given the observed data, so that maximum likelihood estimation on the respondents recovers the population trajectories
key_assumptions.supported_by: Missing-data analyses in Supplementary Tables A1 and A2 comparing responders and non-responders; the authors argue the resulting bias makes their estimates conservative

implies_edges.from: Survey non-response and panel attrition

threats_discussed: Pre-pandemic cohort differences in growth that are not attributable to the pandemic (younger cohorts already declined more steeply)
Differential non-response and panel attrition across cohorts (non-responders in the pandemic cohorts had less educated parents and lower grade-5 well-being)
A higher dropout rate at grade 9 for the pre-pandemic cohort than for the two later cohorts
Divergence from parallel trends between grades 5 and 6
robustness_checks: Models re-estimated including gender, GPA, parental education and immigration status as controls (Table A6): 'This adjustment did not substantially alter the results'
Student fixed-effects regressions (Table A17), which show 'highly similar patterns of change'
unresolved_confounders: Differential non-response and attrition across cohorts, which the authors argue biases their estimates towards being conservative rather than resolving it
Non-parallel trends between grades 5 and 6

estimator.value: Linear mixed-effects (random effects) regression with grade-as-time, estimated by maximum likelihood in Stata 18.1

estimation.specification: Table 2, Model 1a: School Connectedness: outcome regressed on grade-level dummies, cohort dummies (grade effects constrained equal across cohorts)
controls: Grade level dummies for grades 6, 7, 8 and 9 (reference: grade 5)
Cohort dummies for the early-pandemic and full-pandemic cohorts (reference: pre-pandemic cohort)
estimation.clustering: Cluster-adjusted standard errors accounting for students nested in schools

ambiguities: Table 1 reports cohort-specific outcome means on a centred scale (e.g. school connectedness 0.054) but the 'Total' column on the raw 0–4 scale (4.090), so the baseline mean recorded here is the centred/standardised pre-pandemic grade-5 value as printed, not the raw composite.

evidence.annotation: Fig. 2 Outcome trajectories with 95% confidence intervals, by cohort. Note. Measurement points after the onset of the pandemic were grade 9 for the early-pandemic cohort and grades 7, 8 and 9 for the full-pandemic cohort

population.description: DSWQ respondents in the pre-pandemic and early-pandemic cohorts observed in 9th grade and linked to register data on their transition to upper secondary education within two years of finishing 9th grade; the full-pandemic cohort is excluded because transition data were not yet available
population.ages: approximately 15–17 years at the educational transition (9th grade and the following two years)
population.period: 9th-grade DSWQ waves of the pre-pandemic and early-pandemic cohorts (2019 and 2021), with transitions observed within the following two years
population.selection: Annual census-type survey administered during school hours to students in grades 5–9 across Danish public schools, representing approximately 85% of the eligible student population each year; respondents missing all well-being survey waves were excluded, and missing values on the dependent variable were handled by maximum likelihood estimation. The proportion of missing responses varied between 8.22 and 59.93% by wave and cohort. For the educational-choice analyses the sample is further restricted to students for whom a transition could be observed within two years after 9th grade, which excludes the full-pandemic cohort.
